readerTitle: Why you have three delivery apps on your phone
caseNote: 실제 관찰 (여러 배달 앱을 비교하는 소비자, 배달 업계의 적자와 통합 흐름) + 가상 적용 (배달 앱 창업, 청소 업체, 사무실 케이터링)
insight: 배달 앱이 빠르게 성장해도 돈을 벌기 어려운 이유는 손님과 식당이 앱을 쉽게 갈아타고(구매자 교섭력), 비슷한 앱끼리 할인으로 싸우기(경쟁 강도) 때문이며, 두 힘은 서로를 키운다.
misconception: 사용자와 주문이 많으면 결국 수익이 난다. 성장하는 시장이면 좋은 산업이다.

sources.text: Porter, M. (2008). The Five Competitive Forces That Shape Strategy. Harvard Business Review.
주요 배달 플랫폼의 연차 보고서 (예: DoorDash, Deliveroo, Just Eat Takeaway)의 순손실 기록

factChecks.note: 5번 카드의 "여러 대형 배달 기업이 빠른 성장에도 수년간 손실을 보고했다"는 문구는 게시 전에 각사 연차 보고서로 다시 확인하세요. 특정 회사명과 수치는 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
"업계에 인수합병과 철수가 많았다"는 일반적 서술입니다. 예시로 쓸 실제 사례(국가별 철수, 합병)를 확인해 두면 좋습니다. 카드에는 구체 사례를 넣지 않았습니다.
손님과 식당이 여러 앱을 동시에 쓴다는 점(멀티호밍)은 널리 관찰되는 현상이지만 비율 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. 수수료율도 지역마다 달라 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.
7번 카드의 '반복 고객과 직접 거래' 선택지는 플랫폼 약관상 직접 거래 유도가 제한될 수 있어 "where the app's terms allow"를 넣었습니다. 특정 국가의 법률 조언은 아닙니다.

cards.title: Why you have three delivery apps on your phone
body: It's Friday night. You want pad thai from the place down the street. You open one delivery app, then a second, then a third, to see which has the lowest fee tonight.
The restaurant is the same. The food is the same. Only the app changes. That small habit explains a lot about why food delivery is a hard business.

image.label: Phone screen showing the same dish on three different apps
image.brief: 소파에 앉은 사람이 스마트폰을 들고 있고, 화면이 세 칸으로 나뉘어 같은 팟타이 사진과 서로 다른 배달비(예: $1.99, $2.49, $0.99)가 보임. 실제 배달 앱 로고와 색상은 쓰지 않고 가상의 앱 아이콘 3개로 표현.

cards.title: You're launching a delivery app.
body: You plan to launch a food delivery app in a mid-sized city. Two other apps already operate there. Restaurants and diners can use all three.
What will squeeze your profits the most?

options.text: Getting enough restaurants to sign up
options.feedback: A real early hurdle. But restaurants join several apps at once, so signing them is easier than keeping them loyal. That ease is part of the problem.

options.text: Diners and restaurants can switch between apps at almost no cost
options.feedback: That's **buyer power**. When customers can compare and leave in seconds, they keep pushing your fees and commissions down.
Tech costs are real and mostly fixed. They hurt most because they push every app to fight for volume, which is the **rivalry** coming up shortly.

cards.title: Two sets of buyers, both hard to hold.
body: **Buyer power** is how much your customers can push down your prices. It grows when switching is easy and the options look alike.
A delivery app has two sets of buyers. Diners pay delivery fees. Restaurants pay a commission on each order. Both often use several apps at once, so neither is locked in.
Leaving costs a diner one tap. Leaving costs a restaurant one tablet off the counter.

image.label: An app in the middle, pulled by a diner on one side and a restaurant on the other
image.brief: 가운데 가상의 배달 앱 아이콘, 왼쪽에는 휴대폰을 든 손님, 오른쪽에는 주방 앞 식당 주인. 두 사람이 각각 앱을 밧줄로 당기고, 둘 다 뒤쪽에 다른 앱 아이콘 두 개를 들고 있음. 실제 로고 금지.

cards.title: Same restaurants, same food, so fight on price.
body: When every app lists the same restaurants, apps can only compete on fees, discounts and speed. That's intense **rivalry**.

Each app carries large fixed costs: engineers, marketing, customer support. Every extra order helps cover them, so every app wants volume. The fastest way to win volume is a promotion, and rivals answer with their own.

cards.title: The two forces feed each other.
body: Easy switching pushes rivals to compete on discounts. Discounts teach diners to shop for the next deal, which raises their buyer power again. The loop keeps turning.

This helps explain why several large delivery companies reported losses for years despite fast growth, and why the industry has seen many mergers and exits. Growth in orders did not mean growth in profit.

image.label: A loop: easy switching leads to discounts, discounts lead to more deal hunting
image.brief: 원형 화살표 인포그래픽. "Easy switching" → "Apps compete with discounts" → "Diners hunt for deals" → 다시 "Easy switching". 가운데 작은 글씨로 "Orders up, profit flat". 단순한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Forces describe pressure, not fate.
body: This analysis shows the average pull on an industry. A single firm can escape some of it. An app that is the clear leader in one city, or serves a niche like late-night or office orders, may face weaker rivalry there.
Buyer power also differs within each side. A restaurant that diners ask for by name has more power than one of fifty similar pizza places.

cards.title: Now it's a cleaning business.
body: You run a house cleaning company. A booking app sends you new customers but takes a cut of every job. On the app, customers see you next to five other cleaners, sorted by price.

options.text: Lower your price to rank first on the app
options.feedback: You win jobs but feed the **rivalry**. Five similar cleaners on one screen can always undercut each other, and the app still takes its cut.

options.text: Use the app for first jobs, then earn repeat bookings directly where the app's terms allow
options.feedback: On the app, **buyer power** is high because comparing is instant. A trusted regular cleaner is much harder to replace, so that power weakens over time.
You escape the cut and the price comparison, but lose a steady stream of new customers. It works better once you already have enough regulars.

cards.title: Now it's office lunches.
body: You deliver catered lunches to companies. Office managers order weekly, and each quarter they get quotes from three other caterers. A new rival offers 15% less.

options.feedback: This is **rivalry** on price. The rival can cut again, and you've just lowered prices for every client at once.

options.text: Add what's hard to compare: labels for each person's allergies, one monthly invoice, guaranteed on-time delivery
options.feedback: Office managers hold **buyer power** because caterers look alike on a quote. A service that is harder to compare and swap weakens that power and steps out of a pure price fight.

options.text: Ask clients to sign longer contracts at today's price
options.feedback: Contracts slow switching for a while. But if your service still looks identical, buyers will push hard at renewal.

cards.title: A hard industry is one where buyers can leave and rivals look the same.
body: **Concepts used:** buyer power (diners and restaurants switch apps freely) and rivalry (similar apps fighting with discounts). Together they explain why more orders didn't mean more profit.
**Try it today:** ask how easily your customers could compare you with a rival and switch. Then name one thing that makes you harder to swap.
